title: Pay, collections and tips at the Absinthe House; George George
summary: Vincent describes working for collections and set prices at the Absinthe House with T-Ball, then tells how bandleader George George pocketed the money and hired them cheaply.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Ask him when you worked at the Absinthe House.

When did you work at the Absinthe House? It was six. That's when I went to Emris Wright. That's when I told you that me and T-Ball was the darkest man in the band. And the purist man hired his one. They don't make no price with you. They take up collections. If you make a price with them, they give you what the price is. But if you come on just for the kid, sometimes they make $20, $25, $30 a man. But if you tell him $10 a man, they give you $10. Then they come and show you they have about $160 over. And so see if you boys ought to work like I told you. That's a good way. He keep it. Yeah, he keep it. Sometimes they tip us $3 a piece. That's when they used to come in when we'd be lined up and say, what kind of band is this? A white band or what? You know what? You look at me, T-Ball. They say, this is a steel band. There you go. All right, boys. Put it on. And then sometimes I'll come in and give him the room. You know, he'd get broke and come back and borrow a lot of money. And when he'd start to borrow a lot of money, we'd pack up, you know, and leave one by one when he'd get had a drug. We'd go on, you know. That's why we'd come out with about $30 a man, you know. We could make more than that if he wouldn't start to borrow. They don't pay back when they borrow from me. No, that money did. Then sometimes I have a stag. You have to pay for all the purchase like that. You have to make sometimes $40 or $50. You remember George George, I think. Oh, yeah. I'll think about him now. Big old dog fella. Yeah. He just put me in base, but he didn't pay a lot. And when he used to make us. He got the jobs, though. I hope they tell you this. And he could talk to anybody like he wanted, you know. This guy had the white girl's hands. Oh, that's a pretty big letter to me. They pulled a letter to me. And we said, what did you do? I said, beat us up. They knew George was comical, you know. And when George was getting ready to go out, he called the money. And my buddy used to tell me about him how he was, you know. I said, watch old George George. He's crooked. And George George gets the car. He said, I'm going to the laboratory. He said, all right, George. George, count the money. He said, five, six, seven. I said, look, I got a $10 bill. He said, well, didn't I say a $10 bill? And I said, eight, nine. I said, John, that's a $20 bill. He said, well, didn't I say $20? He took all the big money, you know. George, George, go in the back and George, come back. George has $10, $15, $20 bill all up in his necktie. All under his collar like that. You know, cutness, you know. And I told Jack, I said, Jack, you sit up there and go to sleep. You get to the right. Let George, John beat us out all that money like that. I'll rake my hand in a pan, you know. In the kiddo, you have a big dish pan, you know. Just piled up with paper money and silver money. And I tried to get all the paper money I can, because silver money's stuck out. And that old Jack, that old Jack got my treat out of that. Every time he makes it, George come out, he said, that kiddo look mighty slim. He said, somebody's testing the box. I said, ain't nobody on that testing the box. He said, you get all the money. And then George put his back in there, and I said, I had about $50. Who was the other guy? Once he got so stung, though. What Jack, that was Jack Harry? Yeah, Jack, you know, a couple of times. George used to hire different police. Yeah, I know. He'd get a job from the police. I'd work with him once or twice. Yeah, he'd come hire anybody, you know, go out there with him. Couldn't pay a little, because he'd get married with old John. John would be turning up. John would be turning up. And he'd work out here, and I'd say, come with him. You know, he told me, hard tricked him. He told me, he said, I'll get plenty of work. I said, well, yeah, any time you get a job, call me, I'll be right there with you. He said, okay. But he paid me off good. Yeah, yeah. He used to pay off, but you got to watch him, though. Yeah. He called me to cut all the money out. I said, that's all right. I said, I'll take this pile. He used to be, he'd sing all them comical songs, you know. What were the names of the songs he sang? Well, no one of you used to sing about all... When we hung, he just hung by himself. We told him, you don't want to be hung by the band. What's that thing, man? He got to give him his price. His money is dead, you see. And then, let me say, oh, George wants his money, then he's gone. He said, I'm a beehive. That's an animal song. He sing all them comical songs, you know. He sang a song about animals? Did he sing the animal song?
